title: Spiritual Instructions
subtitle: His teaching, told in our words
source: St. Seraphim's teaching, from his conversation with Nicholas Motovilov (1831, first published in 1903) and the Spiritual Instructions gathered from his sayings. No public-domain English of either has been found, so his teaching is told here in our words, never as his own. Scripture is quoted in the King James Version.

sections.title: On the Aim of the Christian Life
paragraphs: St. Seraphim taught that the true aim of the Christian life is the acquisition of the Holy Spirit of God. Fasting, vigils, prayer, almsgiving and every good deed done for Christ's sake are not the aim but the means to it, and only a good deed done for Christ's sake bears the fruit of the Spirit. A good deed not done for His sake, he said, brings no reward in the life to come and no grace in this one, and he pointed to the Lord's word: “he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad” (Matthew 12:30).
So prayer, fasting, vigils and every other Christian labour, however good in themselves, are not the end of the Christian life; they are the means without which it is not reached.
notes: This teaching on the aim of the Christian life comes from his conversation with Nicholas Motovilov, recorded in the winter of 1831 and first published in 1903.

sections.title: On Joy
paragraphs: He taught that no one should give way to despondency, even when his sins are great. Despondency robs the soul of its strength and of all hope of salvation, while the merciful Lord has given in His Mysteries every help we need, and nothing can withstand His grace when we turn to Him.
Above all he counselled peace of soul: the one who acquires a peaceful spirit, he taught, will see thousands around him saved.
notes: His saying on acquiring a peaceful spirit is the most quoted of all his words, repeated in nearly every Russian spiritual handbook of the 19th and 20th centuries. With no public-domain English of it, it is told here in our words.

sections.title: On the Jesus Prayer
paragraphs: He counselled prayer at every time and in every place: walking, sitting, at work, and in church before the service begins. Going about one's duties, one may repeat “Lord, have mercy”, and when weakness does not allow it always, as often as one can.
The Lord, he taught, hears the monk and the layman, the wise and the simple alike, if they are sound and true Orthodox Christians, and gives His grace to both when they repent and pray with faith.
notes: The counsel to keep “Lord, have mercy” throughout the day reflects the older hesychast tradition of unceasing prayer (1 Thessalonians 5:17).
